  • A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.
  • Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Watch: Inside court as Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 19 years over assassination plot.

A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge stated he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.

He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

In a recent development, nikhil Gupta (seen in a 2024 courtroom sketch) pleaded guilty in a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a U.S. resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in Latest York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors noted.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors mentioned. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in Upcoming York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton remarked in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs stated that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.

The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson mentioned.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed.".

Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader.

Who was Canadian Sikh leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar?

Why are some Sikhs calling for a separate state?

Canada accuses India of role in Sikh leader's murder.

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.

Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.

In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun remarked the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.

"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.

Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau remarked there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.

According to recent reports, nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.

The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets.".

  • Recent findings suggest that cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35.

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Recent findings suggest that cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

We’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

#58805. Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1137 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
  • The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
  • Sources indicate that update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end people and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Sources indicate that update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

It has been revealed that each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were rapidly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

It has been revealed that as noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

It has been revealed that last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

Recent findings suggest that the clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically demonstrated up two or three days after the request.

In a recent development, this wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

It has been revealed that the researcher stated he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

    • California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    State attorney indicates scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors.

    California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

    Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based firm’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

    “The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the firm may have misled investors,” said Bonta.

    “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”.

    The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

    Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.

    Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the firm late last year.

    Bonta remarked the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

    Recent findings suggest that “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”.

    Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

    Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, remarked the tech giant had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.

    Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

    Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.

    The tech giant, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

    In a recent development, hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.

    AMD noted the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

    “AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the manufacturer mentioned. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”.

    AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

    Trump claims he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US.

    Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

    "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

    Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

    Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

    "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

    "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen.".

    But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

    Sources indicate that "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even stated that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

    Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

    It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

    Washington on Monday declared firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

    The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

    Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back.

    Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

    As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

    Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about complications including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

    According to recent reports, "You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

    Industry observers note that "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets.".

    Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

    Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

    The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

    In September Google announced a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

    Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

    Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

    Google has been contacted for comment.

    #58801. Discs vs. disks: What's the difference?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (507 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Discs vs. disks: What's the difference?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There are more things that set them apart than spelling.
    • In a recent development, one of the key parts of understanding technology and its many eccentricities comes from understanding the actual language being used and discerning the unique, subtle differences a letter can make in a word.
    • If you've been around tech for any amount of time, you've most likely come into contact with the word disc.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There are more things that set them apart than spelling.

    In a recent development, one of the key parts of understanding technology and its many eccentricities comes from understanding the actual language being used and discerning the unique, subtle differences a letter can make in a word. It may not seem like much, but something as simple as a changed letter can do a lot of heavy lifting for certain pieces of technology.

    If you've been around tech for any amount of time, you've most likely come into contact with the word disc. Or perhaps you saw it spelled as disk, concluding with a K instead of a C. It may seem like a curious case of the Queen's English contrasting with American spelling, but it's actually a bit more complicated than that.

    Sources indicate that though they share similarities in some ways, the two spellings often refer to different types of technologies. It can be confusing, but once you understand the distinctions, it becomes clear how each one is different from the other.

    According to recent reports, to put it simply, the two spellings of disk and disc refer to traditional magnetic storage vs. optical storage media. They share similar modalities and functions, but the spelling of each one is indicative of what type of media you're dealing with.

    Sources indicate that disk with a K generally refers to magnetic storage, such as older mechanical hard drives and floppy disks. You likely have noticed the word spelled this way on your computer, as it refers to your hard drive as disks. While SSDs are also identified with the word disk, they're not technically disks in the traditional sense, as a majority of them use NAND flash memory as opposed to moving, mechanical parts.

    Recent findings suggest that A disc, with a C at the end, is usually in reference to optical storage formats. This is what you may find when you open a video game, if it even has a disc these days, of course, or a DVD. If you look on the back of a Blu-ray case, you'll notice it refers to itself as a disc. If you buy a music CD, you'll notice that it is also referred to as a compact disc as opposed to disk.

    Industry observers note that it may seem tempting to wonder whether, on a technicality, using the terms interchangeably wouldn't be entirely incorrect. While it's not likely to get you yelled at, a disk and a disc serve two distinct functions with form factors that sometimes feel like they do the same thing.

    If you're transferring files on your computer, downloading them from the internet or inserting a floppy into an older PC, you're making use of a disk. On the contrary, if you're putting a video game into a console or a DVD into a player, what you're using is a disc. Both are designed to store and display data and files, but the way they work is fundamentally different from each other.

    It has been revealed that the company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.

    Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

    #58793. The trade-offs of using Apple's AirPods Max headphones

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (741 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    The trade-offs of using Apple's AirPods Max headphones

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple's AirPods Max sound great, but they come with a lot of compromises for $549 headphones.
    • There's a lot to love about the AirPods Max, Apple's premium headphones that recently got a nice revision with improved ANC and the H2 chip.
    • The AirPods Max are quite heavy compared to their main competitors, and that might bother some people.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple's AirPods Max sound great, but they come with a lot of compromises for $549 headphones.

    There's a lot to love about the AirPods Max, Apple's premium headphones that recently got a nice revision with improved ANC and the H2 chip. For iPhone customers, they definitely play nicely with the Apple ecosystem thanks to features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness and Live Translation, not to mention that the audio quality is really good. But the AirPods Max aren't perfect. At $549, they're too expensive for headphones that haven't changed much since 2020. They're also heavy and come with a clunky case. If you've been thinking about buying the AirPods Max, there are a few trade-offs you definitely need to consider before making your decision.

    The AirPods Max are quite heavy compared to their main competitors, and that might bother some people. It's true that they have a super-premium design made of aluminum and steel, but all that adds up to 386 grams (13.6 ounces). By comparison, the mostly plastic Beats 360 weigh only 294 grams (10.4 ounces) and definitely feel lighter when you wear them for more than an hour. Wearing the AirPods Max for long periods of time, like during a long flight, can really make you aware of that extra bulk.

    Sources indicate that although they're made with premium materials, the AirPods Max's design is also a bit clunky, especially when it comes to the Smart Case. There's no power button on the AirPods Max. Instead, they rely on the Smart Case to enter sleep mode — which has magnets to tell the headphones that they're stored away and not in use. The thing is, Apple's Smart Case doesn't really protect the AirPods Max. The headband stays exposed and it can easily be damaged if you throw your headphones into a backpack with anything sharp. The ear cups aren't fully protected either. The headphones also don't fold up (only the ear cups rotate flat), so they take up a lot of space in a bag.

    Sources indicate that there are many complaints about the AirPods Max headband peeling over time — and since the AirPods Max 2 have exactly the same design as the first generation, it's very unlikely that anything has changed here. There are third-party cases for the AirPods Max that include the magnets needed to put the headphones into sleep mode, but you'll have to spend a few extra dollars on top of the $549 price to fix a design flaw.

    In a recent development, another major complaint about the AirPods Max is condensation inside the ear cups. A lawsuit filed in 2025 claimed that this moisture could degrade sound quality and cause the ear detection feature to malfunction over time, although a judge later dismissed the case. This problem persists with the AirPods Max 2, and iFixit indicates there are no visible changes to the internal seals — although Apple claims that the moisture is easy to spot and clean since the ear cups are easily removable. Still, it's something to keep in mind.

    In a recent development, repairing the AirPods Max is also very difficult. It's not impossible, unlike the smaller AirPods, but taking the headphones apart requires specialized tools and removing a lot of adhesive strips. Apple charges $79 for battery replacements, and that's the only repair the company offers. If any other hardware component fails, Apple replaces the headphones with a newly introduced pair, and that service typically costs around $300. For that price, you can buy a good pair of new headphones — like the new Beats 360, which compare to the AirPods Max in many ways. You are able to replace the ear pads yourself as needed, since these snap on and off easily. A pair of those will cost you $69, unless you opt for a third-party option.

    For audiophiles, the AirPods Max also seem to fall a little short. It's not that they sound bad — they actually sound great. But they still lack codecs for high-res audio over Bluetooth, so you'll need a USB-C cable to get lossless audio. Many other premium headphones on the market already support codecs such as LDAC and aptX HD for higher audio quality over Bluetooth.

    Industry observers note that when you put it all in perspective, the AirPods Max seem way too expensive for what they offer. It's a good product, but it's not exceptional for $549.

Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he remarked, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”.

    Industry observers note that according to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.

    In a recent development, naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been stated, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

    Latest Update: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
    • The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta.
    • “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Substantial Tech competitor racing to build newly introduced AI data centers.

    The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”.

    “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

    Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

    Industry observers note that but all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

    Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

    That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and Upcoming Hampshire. The organization attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

    That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

    Recent findings suggest that for comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

    Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

    Industry observers note that but even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

    From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

    Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

    Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

    Industry observers note that still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”.

    It would very much be in the public interest for other Significant Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

    President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and states he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi.

    Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

    In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

    Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

    At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

    “We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

    He noted Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

    “You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he noted.

    “We want them to build it here.”.

    With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

    The Trump administration on Monday issued upcoming rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

    China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

    It has been revealed that in the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”.

    It has been revealed that he added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”.

    Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

    According to recent reports, “I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president remarked. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”.

    Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

    Industry observers note that “I can’t speak to America,” he mentioned, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”.

    He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

    “I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

    Industry observers note that trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”.

    According to recent reports, and he mentioned Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”.

    Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.

    From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

    If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.

    According to recent reports, the AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.

    You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.

    Recent findings suggest that the Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.

    Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work, is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.

    Recent findings suggest that priced at $159 (at the moment reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.

    The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.

    If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).

    Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.

    The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.

    Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the tech giant’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.

    According to recent reports, starting at $479, the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas.

    Industry observers note that notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries.

    If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you.

    According to recent reports, priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls.

    The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls.

    Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday.

    Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits.

    The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Karen Scarborough (left) and Anne Lindboe got to work with a two-handled saw.
    • This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
    • In a recent development, the 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Karen Scarborough (left) and Anne Lindboe got to work with a two-handled saw.

    This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.

    In a recent development, the 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

    Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.

    Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.

    Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.

    "This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period.".

    The 21m tree has been nicknamed Jolly Cheery.

    Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square.".

    Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.

    "The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.

    "I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times.".

    Count the rings: Anne Lindboe (left) and Karen Scarborough (right) with a slice of the 75-year-old trunk.

    For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.

    Organisers mentioned it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.

    Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    What's new with Apple's latest Siri Remote, and does your old Apple TV support it?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the 4th-gen Apple TV 4K comes with a new remote.
    • Earlier this October, Apple unveiled its latest Apple TV 4K streaming box.
    • Recent findings suggest that one of the most underrated aspects of the latest Apple TV 4K is the introduction of its new remote.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the 4th-gen Apple TV 4K comes with a new remote. Here's what you need to know about it.

    Earlier this October, Apple unveiled its latest Apple TV 4K streaming box. Like most product launches in recent months, the release centered around a "supercharged" AI offering, which Apple believes will transform "how people search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience." In its announcement, Apple touted the AI-enabled fourth generation of its popular streaming hub as the "most immersive home theater experience yet.".

    Recent findings suggest that one of the most underrated aspects of the latest Apple TV 4K is the introduction of its new remote. At first glance, the Siri Remote doesn't appear much different. Sporting the same sleek silver and black design fashioned with 100 percent recycled aluminum, it retains the touch-enabled clickpad and voice recognition from its previous version. Like its third-generation predecessor, the new Siri Remote uses a USB-C port for quick recharging and better cross-compatibility.

    Industry observers note that however, the latest Siri Remote builds on top of this beloved design by adding a more precise Find My feature. With Precision Finding, you can use your phone's Find My app to find exactly where your fourth-gen Siri Remote is hiding. The remote also adds the ability to play a sound when trying to locate it, much to the joy of those affected by the couch-swallowing gremlins plaguing America's living rooms.

    In a recent development, the upcoming Apple TV 4K is now on available for purchase, and the new Siri Remote comes in the box. However, you will also be able purchase the fourth-generation Siri Remote separately via Apple's website or at your local Apple Store.

    Sources indicate that retailing for $59, the remote is compatible with all four generations of the Apple TV 4K, as well as the Apple TV HD. Those holding onto Apple TV models from before 2015 will need to continue digging through their couch cushions.

    This expanded compatibility is notable given Apple's looks for Siri AI. As it stands, the fine print of Apple's press release notes that the new AI suite isn't exclusive to the new streaming box. Instead, the organization is also pushing its Siri AI features to both Apple TV 4K's second- and third-generation boxes. So while you might be tempted to upgrade your streaming box in order to benefit from the faster speeds, an Ethernet port and a built-in microphones, you may also find that upgrading your Apple TV 4K simply isn't worth the $299 price tag. As such, you may want to consider simply upgrade your remote separately and save $240.

    There is a catch, however. In addition to a compatible streaming device, your fourth-gen Siri Remote will need to be paired with a relatively new iPhone to unlock its Precision Finding feature. As it stands, the feature is available to Apple viewers with an iPhone Duo, iPhone Air, or iPhone 17 or later, except the iPhone 17e. You will also need to run Apple's latest iOS software, iOS 27.

    According to recent reports, similar to people with a second- or third-generation Siri Remote, those with an older iPhone will be able to use Apple's Find My feature without Precision Finding. This may be a surprise, as Apple's iPhone 15 and 16 models support Precision Finding for products like the AirTag 2. However, some speculate that this is because Apple's Find My tech has transitioned from using its Ultra Wideband chip to Bluetooth 6 technology in this instance.

    Apple promises that its Siri AI will make your Apple TV 4K more helpful and intuitive by adding a "profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions.".

    Siri AI allows you to ask your television questions like, "Siri, who won Best Comedy at this year's Emmy Awards?" You can also ask Siri questions about the film or show you are watching, such as filming locations, why recognize a particular actor or whether a movie is appropriate for your children. Responses are overlaid at the corner of your screen in order to not disrupt your viewing experience.

    In service of this mission, the box has three far-field microphones, extending your hands-free viewing experience across the room. Moreover, advanced echo cancellation allows your Apple TV 4K to isolate your voice and block out the noise, ensuring you don't spend half the show unsuccessfully screaming at Siri. This also means you don't have to speak all of your queries into the Siri Remote; the box itself can hear you.

    The new Apple TV 4K also promises significant speed gains. By adding a new A19 chip, Apple claims that its latest streaming box will achieve 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to twice the GPU speeds when compared to its third-gen predecessor. Its AV1 decoder will enable more bandwidth-efficient streams, increasing visual quality without overloading your network.

    Sources indicate that connected to a four compatible HomePods, you can achieve Apple's best surround sound experience. Moreover, you can manage smart home hub notifications with AI-generated camera activity descriptions, doorbell notifications and enhanced control of select accessories.

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey.
    • A upcoming draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'.
    • Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey.

    A upcoming draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'.

    Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached.

    These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21:.

    Harjeet Singh, the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, stated that COP31 could be a failure due to a lack of funding.

    It has been revealed that "COP31 is stuck for one simple reason: money. Europe and other rich countries came to Antalya with empty pockets," he wrote in a statement shared with multiple reporters.

    "They've spent two weeks pushing electrification targets and demanding more ambition from developing countries, while refusing to pay for any of it," he added.

    Singh accused wealthy countries of blocking a just transition mechanism and of ignoring calls to increase funding for the Adaptation Fund and the Loss and Damage Fund.

    "You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he wrote.

    Sources indicate that the climate activist stressed that the reason this COP failed wasn't a lack of solutions. It was due to "a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis," he mentioned.

    According to recent reports, carbon capture technology works, but its real-world capabilities are nowhere near to moving the needle on climate change. So what's the hold-up?

    Attacks on climate science and disinformation seem to be delaying key decisions as the UN climate talks draw to a close in Antalya.

    Leaders from Africa, one of the continents worst hit by climate change, have spent years lobbying for hundreds of billions of dollars to help adapt to the rising impacts of global warming.

    The rest of the world relies on African nations for their abundant natural resources, many of them used in clean energy production.

    Yet at COP31, wealthy nations have so far failed to commit to the financing needed to help developing nations make a just transition.

    Read our report from DW’s Kathy Wood.

    The head of Peru's delegation at COP31, Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, warned that the UN climate summit was unlikely to end with a concrete deal on climate financing or cutting fossil fuel use.

    Garrido Sanchez lamented that the outcome "would be very limited.".

    He reiterated how "geopolitical divisions" were stopping any final deal from mentioning reducing reliance on oil, gas and coal.

    The Peruvian delegate singled out major oil producers, such as Gulf Arab states and Russia, as showing significant opposition.

    He noted that while Latin American neighbor Panama had also signaled objection to including the term fossil fuels in the final text, Peru was "not so radical" and is keen to attract investment to "ensure our energy security" through renewables.

    China has backed a plan proposed by COP host Turkey to raise global electricity demand to 35% by 2035 — up from the current 20%.

    Industry observers note that in a joint statement with Australia, which is leading negotiations between almost 200 nations at the COP31 summit in Turkey, Beijing said it welcomes "growing international ambition and cooperation ... to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 on a voluntary basis.".

    The statement goes on to highlight the benefits the transition can bring for the economy, jobs, energy security, public health and households.

    The two partners also "acknowledge the importance of inclusive climate action that ensures no one is left behind," the text continued.

    Dozens of countries, including EU states, Japan, South Korea and Canada, have so far signaled support for the voluntary goal, which aims to boost clean energy use.

    Yet, environmental groups have warned that the draft text doesn't stipulate the use of solar, wind and other renewable energy sources, which could allow power plants using natural gas and coal to be included.

    China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.
    • China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has mentioned.
    • Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, mentioned: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.

    China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has mentioned.

    Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, mentioned: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”.

    China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

    But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

    It has been revealed that in an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang stated: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”.

    Experts have remarked electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

    While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

    Sources indicate that but campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

    In a recent development, last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

    Industry observers note that wang remarked China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

    According to recent reports, china still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

    According to recent reports, one of the key challenges at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

    Industry observers note that wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”.

    China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

    Recent findings suggest that some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

    Wang called for more work on trade concerns at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”.

    Sources indicate that jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”.

    Recent findings suggest that negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a newly introduced draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

    #58777. Tech Report: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

    Tech Report: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A transcription manufacturer that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.
    • Industry observers note that the data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage.
    • According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A transcription manufacturer that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

    Industry observers note that the data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the tech giant’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

    According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

    The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

    Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the organization to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

    Recent findings suggest that sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”.

    Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

    Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

    It has been revealed that “We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, remarked in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”.

    “We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

    The manufacturer remarked that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

    Industry observers note that it’s unclear if the firm has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

    It has been revealed that discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

    The modern web runs on absolute trust, he said, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

    Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen said that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

    “An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

    Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the upcoming wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

    Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.

    According to recent reports, “Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”.

    Mamdani confirms plan to close Newly introduced York's Rikers Island jail by 2032

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years.
    • Upcoming York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new initiative from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
    • Mamdani on Friday unveiled a blueprint to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four fresh jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years.

    Upcoming York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new initiative from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

    Mamdani on Friday unveiled a blueprint to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four fresh jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

    According to recent reports, plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

    Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

    It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she noted.

    The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

    It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

    "[B]uilding a newly introduced system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges.".

    "It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in Fresh York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.

    It has been revealed that the jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.

    Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.

    In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.

    Newly introduced York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the blueprint.

    Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

    The mayor's office argues the newly introduced, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

    Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across Latest York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.

    He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health challenges.

    Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.

    The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (Â£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.
