    • In a recent development, christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse.

    A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

    In a recent development, christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.

    He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.

    Recent findings suggest that federal prosecutors noted south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

    Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.

    Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.

    Sources indicate that haiti has not had a president since authorities mentioned that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.

    The election of a newly introduced president is scheduled for next year.

    Prosecutors stated the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

    Recent findings suggest that the plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

    CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials mentioned.

    By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.

    Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

    Industry observers note that intuit acquired the tech giant in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

    Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the fresh cash will be used to repurchase shares.

    Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

    Sources indicate that still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the tech giant has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

    “We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," mentioned Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

    Sources indicate that the government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    According to recent reports, the importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the matter: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

    At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world.".

    According to recent reports, the German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Recent findings suggest that regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

    According to recent reports, in China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

    One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    In a recent development, the reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.

    It has been revealed that the report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

    Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

    These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

    China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

    Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the matter accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

    It has been revealed that in doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

    In a recent development, one example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental complications relating to religion and foreign policy.".

    How to easily factory reset your Fitbit

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It can help fix a serious issue or prep your wearable for a fresh owner.
    • Industry observers note that if your Fitbit is acting up, you'll want to restart it, but this is a very different process from a factory reset.
    • There are only a few times you'll want to factory reset a Fitbit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It can help fix a serious issue or prep your wearable for a fresh owner.

    Industry observers note that if your Fitbit is acting up, you'll want to restart it, but this is a very different process from a factory reset. You may want to restart your Fitbit if it won't sync with the Google Health app or isn't registering data. However, if the screen is unresponsive to taps or swipes, or it's frozen on a specific screen, you can force a hard restart, which typically involves pressing and holding a button (or buttons) for a specific period of time until the screen resets. How to restart your Fitbit device varies by model. It's a refresh, like turning something off and on again. A factory reset, on the other hand, removes all unsynced settings and data from the device and brings the wearable back to its original state when it was first purchased.

    There are only a few times you'll want to factory reset a Fitbit. Do this if you're giving it to someone else or selling it. It's also worth doing for data privacy, if the device is no longer functioning properly and you're dropping it off for safe recycling. Finally, it's a last-ditch effort if a restart isn't fixing a major issue. Factory resetting your Fitbit is simple, but use this option only when necessary.

    For Fitbits with a screen, go to Settings > About > Device Info > Clear User Data or Factory Reset. You may need to hold down a button on the screen to confirm, and you should feel a slight vibration when it's done and the Fitbit logo reappears on-screen. With the newest Fitbit Edge, it's even easier: swipe down from the top of the screen and select Settings > Clear User Data.

    Industry observers note that with older Fitbit trackers, you may have to connect the device to its charger and hold down a button or use a paperclip. With the Fitbit Flex, for example, which does not have a screen, connect the sensor to its charger, plug the charger into your computer via USB, find the black reset hole, and press it for three seconds with a paperclip. Wait for it to light up and confirm the reset.

    It has been revealed that interestingly, the new screenless Fitbit Air (see our Fitbit Air review) does not have a traditional factory reset option. Instead, place it on its charger and press and hold the back button for 10 seconds (or until the status light flashes white). This will restart the device. If a new user pairs with the wearable, your account data will be cleared automatically.

    It's a good idea to manually unpair a Fitbit Air from your account first if you're handing it off. In the app, select the device from the top-left corner and, under System, select Disconnect & reset device. If it's not connecting to a new phone, forget it from your phone's Bluetooth menu (Settings > Bluetooth > tap the "i" beside the device and select Forget This Device.

    Industry observers note that A factory reset is a last-resort option. I recently had concerns syncing my Fitbit Edge with my iPhone; it got stuck in a boot loop and froze on a specific screen. Nothing I tried worked until I tried a factory reset.

    It's key to reiterate that a factory reset will erase all data that is stored locally on the device. This could include morning alarms, goals, notification settings, and any unsynced activities. It does not, however, delete data that's already been synced to the Google Health app. After resetting my Fitbit Edge, for example, all my daily data, including steps, workouts, and more, were still accessible in the app.

    If you're holding onto an older, discontinued Fitbit model and it's still working, look for instructions on how to factory reset it in the supporting documentation online, or check the Help menu in the Google Health app. Whichever model you have, once the factory reset process is done, it's like a upcoming device again, and you can start the pairing and syncing process from scratch. Be patient: It may take some time to start accurately tracking your data again.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

    Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the upcoming desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

    The search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

    According to recent reports, the other major change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

    Sources indicate that it’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that reveals that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

    In a recent development, this change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week.

    An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the manufacturer's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

    Levent AlpÃ¶ge noted, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

    It has been revealed that if found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

    The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

    As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

    It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

    Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

    Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

    AlpÃ¶ge mentioned that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

    "The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge mentioned, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier.".

    "I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

    The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

    Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, stated on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

    "I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao remarked.

    No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

    OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

    More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

    The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

    Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

    A group of maths scholars mentioned, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

    "We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

    A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

    It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

    #58765. Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (672 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit.
    • The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
    • Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

    The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

    Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that but you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the organization’s orbital data center aims. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

    That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

    It has been revealed that however, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

    It has been revealed that musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

    Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

    That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

    Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1125 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.
    • In a recent development, the race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the substantial powers.
    • Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.

    In a recent development, the race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the substantial powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

    Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

    Industry observers note that despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

    The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially vital since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.

    One diplomat mentioned: “The electoral system means it is key how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”.

    The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

    Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

    Industry observers note that A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious substantial-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

    Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

    In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

    Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

    In a recent development, some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, presently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

    Industry observers note that but others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

    It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

    Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

    The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

    In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.

    In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

    According to recent reports, grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

    It has been revealed that although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.

    One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

    #58763. How long can fiber optic cables be before they lose signal?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (749 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    How long can fiber optic cables be before they lose signal?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, fiber optic cables are responsible for a significant portion of the world's Internet infrastructure.
    • The longest fiber optic cable run in the world is the 2Africa cable system.
    • It has been revealed that as with any technology, fiber-optic cables have their limits.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, fiber optic cables are responsible for a significant portion of the world's Internet infrastructure. You may know that the technology is responsible for carrying data signals across oceans, but fiber has also become increasingly common in our cities and even homes. Many internet service providers (ISPs) use fiber-optic as a selling point, and for good reason: It offers a significant internet speed upgrade over legacy DSL connections that rely on copper telephone lines.

    The longest fiber optic cable run in the world is the 2Africa cable system. It's an underwater optical fiber cable that has landing points in many African countries as well as Europe and Asia. The previous record was held by SEA-ME-WE 3, a cable system that connected portions of Europe, Northern Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and Australia. That system was decommissioned in 2024.

    It has been revealed that as with any technology, fiber-optic cables have their limits. So how long can a fiber-optic cable actually be before signal loss makes the data being transmitted completely unrecoverable?

    Sources indicate that fiber-optic cables rely on a physics principle called total internal reflection to transmit data through glass (or sometimes plastic) strands in the form of light. The glass core has a high enough refractive index so that when light hits the boundary at a sufficiently shallow angle, it reflects back into the core rather than passing through. This allows the light to travel long distances without experiencing significant energy loss or signal deterioration.

    In a recent development, this is in stark contrast to Ethernet cables, which rely on twisted pairs of copper wires to transmit data in the form of electrical current. Like any metallic conductor, copper wires have some resistance, which means you can't use them for very long distances. The maximum recommended length for Cat5e Ethernet cables is just 100 meters or slightly over 300 feet. They're also affected by electromagnetic interference, affecting their reliability over long runs.

    According to recent reports, by comparison, fiber optic cables can carry data over several kilometers before the signal starts breaking down. A single fiber-optic cable can bundle multiple individual fibers, each capable of carrying its own data signals. This is why internet service providers advertise their use of fiber over traditional copper wiring when deploying city-wide networks. The end result is a much faster connection that's often more consistent.

    It has been revealed that however, fiber optic cables have limits too. Even with total internal reflection, a small amount of light is lost as it travels through the glass core due to absorption and scattering. This gradual reduction in signal strength is called attenuation. Over a long enough run, this weakens the signal until the receiver can no longer distinguish between useful data and noise.

    Recent findings suggest that A single uninterrupted glass fiber can typically span several kilometers before signal loss becomes a limiting factor. Keep in mind, fiber-optic cables also come in two types: single-mode and multi-mode.

    Recent findings suggest that single-mode fiber only allows one beam of light to travel through it at a time, while multi-mode fiber allows multiple light pulses (called modes) to propagate through the strands simultaneously. These pulses take slightly different paths within the strand, which means they can arrive at different times. This is called modal dispersion and eventually causes the receiver to struggle interpreting the data signal.

    Single-mode fiber is capable of carrying signals over longer distances but requires specific equipment that can cost significantly more money. Multi-mode fiber cables have wider cores that makes optical alignment with transceiver equipment easier, so they're often the preferred choice for shorter fiber runs. With longer runs, though, single-mode fiber's stability can justify the higher equipment costs.

    Regardless of the operating mode, you likely won't have to worry about signal loss in a typical home network. Even multi-mode fiber can cover hundreds of meters. The bigger problem in a domestic fiber cable run is often caused by bends that are too tight, which can cause light leakage from the core.

    In a recent development, in the case of fiber optic systems running across continents, they use optical amplifiers to compensate for signal loss over long distances. These devices are installed along the seabed and designed to boost the optical signal. A technique known as multiplexing then allows multiple data streams to travel simultaneously over a single strand. Put simply: You never have a truly uninterrupted fiber optic cable running over such vast distances.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: Miliband spoke to the BBC following the summit in Brussels.

    A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

    The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a latest youth mobility scheme.

    However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

    Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband noted "all the options will be on the table".

    It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

    What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

    Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more.

    Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow.

    UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.

    The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.

    EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

    Miliband remarked it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

    "President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She noted there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.

    Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely.".

    "The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely.".

    Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.

    He remarked previously revealed agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".

    Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

    Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

    He remarked that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

    Recent findings suggest that "Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

    Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

    She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the Â£17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

    Reform UK leader Nigel Farage stated Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

    Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud.".

    Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey noted there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

    Recent findings suggest that "A youth mobility scheme is a major step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole newly introduced deal that actually works for Britain, and fast.".

    Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison stated closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the glitch of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".

    He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take Â£500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".

    He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway.".

    Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.

    She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals.".

    • Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.

    The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

    Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.

    An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

    Sources indicate that the secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

    Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

    Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.

    XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

    Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.

    Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

    The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

    In a recent development, in both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

    According to recent reports, investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

    In a recent development, as with any fresh technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO2-cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.

    That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

    Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025.

    A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

    Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.

    The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.

    Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.

    Jonathan Rinderknecht's arrest in October last year.

    Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

    One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

    "We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," mentioned Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

    Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

    Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.

    Lawyers for the defendant remarked they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.

    Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, noted in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".

    In a recent development, "So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality.".

    Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.

    They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that demonstrated his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.

    They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.

    The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

    • The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.
    • In a recent development, “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S.
    • In a recent development, CNN first reported the letter’s existence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

    In a recent development, “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

    In a recent development, CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

    SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

    During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

    Industry observers note that on October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

    It has been revealed that the central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has said that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

    “My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”.

    The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

    “It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

    Sources indicate that various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

    It seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or introduces, as the company is currently providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

    AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that it’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab.
    • “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
    • The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that it’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most notable problems in mathematics.

    “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

    The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

    Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this ….

    The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

    For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

    But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

    It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

    Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

    Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”.

    However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.

    Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another crucial proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.

    Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”.

    Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.

    In a recent development, in a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”.

    This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.

    Russian  ballistic missile strikes on Ukraine's southern city of Kryvyi Rih — President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown — killed two people and wounded dozens of others, local officials said Saturday.

    The attacks come amid little progress in talks to end the nearly five-year-old war and after Ukraine, on three occasions this week, struck the Kerch bridge linking Russian-occupied Crimea with Russia.

    Russian President Vladimir Putin had vowed a "painful" response to the Kerch attack, as the bridge is vital for war supplies for Russian forces in the south.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Among the dead in Friday evening's double-tap strikes on Kryvyi Rih were a 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while several children were among the 60 wounded, the Ukrainian officials noted.

    Several fires broke out and damage was caused to about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram.

    Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.

    Russia's Defense Ministry said a thermal power plant in the city was hit, along with a power substation in the region of Rivne, on the opposite side of the country.

    Both facilities supply electricity to the industry supporting Ukraine's military, the ministry added.

    Elsewhere in the nearly five-year-long war, Russia ​also struck a ​cargo vessel ‌near Odesa, which Moscow said was carrying dual-use goods ​for ⁠the Ukrainian military.

    Eleven people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service noted Saturday.

    One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.

    In Russia, local officials mentioned Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

    Finland, meanwhile, said it detected a drone attack on Saturday morning on a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea, prompting Prime Minister Petteri Orpo to warn that the war is "spilling over into our immediate vicinity.".

    After damage to Russia's Kerch bridge to Crimea, Zelenskyy warned in an interview with US broadcaster NBC that the structure "will not remain standing anyway.".
